speaker: Nick Kokonas
title: Nick Kokonas on Resurrecting Restaurants, Skin in the Game, and Investing
question: In hospitality ticketing platforms, why does paying merchants before an event takes place create severe downside risk?
guest: About three years ago we were assessing our clearing risk. Tock not only does ordinary reservations, we sell tickets to events for restaurants or special tables like chef's tables or prix fixe menus, about $30 to $40 million a month around the world. One of the things we have to assess is the risk of how we pay those restaurants out. It's the Fyre Festival scenario: you sell all the tickets ahead of time, pay out the money to the promoter, and if the event doesn't take place or they disappear with the money, we're left holding the bag. It's a bit like running a clearing firm. Our CFO, Steve Bernacki, said to me, 'We shouldn't pay out restaurants this far in advance because there's risk they can default.' And I said in an email, 'It's not like every restaurant in America can close all at once.' I was wrong about that. Even if the probability of a widespread shutdown looks very low—maybe 5 or 10 percent—if it does happen, it's existential blowout risk. Tock could wake up on the hook for $5 to $10 million, which would blow the company up.

points.core: Advancing ticket payouts makes the platform liable if merchants fail to deliver.
points.note: Accept: platform absorbs refund or chargeback liability like a clearing firm when a restaurant or event organizer defaults after early payout. Do not credit: vague mentions of merchant fraud without explaining who bears the financial loss.

points.core: Correlated industry-wide closures can trigger simultaneous defaults that overwhelm platform reserves.
points.note: Accept: systemic shocks shutting many merchants at once turn manageable individual default rates into existential blowout liability. Do not credit: generic statements that economic downturns reduce platform revenue.

points.core: Assuming merchant defaults stay independent masks catastrophic tail risk during systemic shocks.
points.note: Accept: believing all merchants cannot fail simultaneously underprices correlated counterparty risk across large prepaid ticket volumes. Do not credit: generic risk-management platitudes or advice to diversify.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Paying merchants before the event means the platform has released funds for a service that hasn't yet been delivered, while it remains financially liable to the ticket buyers.

If the event is cancelled, postponed, or the organiser becomes insolvent or commits fraud, customers are entitled to refunds and can file chargebacks with their card issuers. Those claims land on the platform (as merchant of record or payment facilitator), not on the organiser who already has the money. The platform must then refund from its own balance sheet and try to claw back funds from a merchant who may have spent them, gone bankrupt, or disappeared.

The risk is severe for a few reasons. Tickets are sold weeks or months ahead, so exposure accumulates over a long window. Losses are also correlated: a single large event failing, or a systemic shock like COVID-19, triggers mass refunds at once. And the platform earns only a small fee per ticket but bears the full face value as loss, so one failure can wipe out the margin from many successful events.

This is why platforms typically use escrow, rolling reserves, delayed payouts, or merchant underwriting.

points.why: The response explains that after an early payout, the platform must fund customer refunds even if it cannot recover the money from the merchant.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Paying merchants before an event occurs turns a ticketing platform into an unsecured creditor bearing unfulfilled-delivery risk. Ticket buyers often pay weeks or months ahead, while hospitality operators typically spend advance payouts immediately on non-recoverable upfront costs like venue deposits, talent, staffing, and catering. If an event is canceled, postponed, poorly executed, or fraudulent, buyers demand refunds or initiate credit card chargebacks. Under card-network rules, the platform, as merchant of record or payment facilitator, remains directly liable for refunding the full purchase price and paying dispute fees even after disbursing the cash. Because thinly capitalized merchants rarely have the liquidity to return spent funds and may become insolvent, recoupment frequently fails. This creates severe loss asymmetry: the platform earns only a small percentage fee per ticket, yet risks losing 100% of gross ticket value plus network penalties. Worse, correlated shocks such as severe weather, venue closures, or pandemics can trigger mass cancellations simultaneously, rapidly draining the platform’s own liquidity and jeopardizing its card-processing standing.

noweb.answer: Paying merchants before an event occurs transforms a ticketing platform from a fee-collecting intermediary into an unsecured lender bearing asymmetric counterparty risk. Organizers routinely spend advance payouts immediately on non-recoverable upfront costs like venue deposits, talent fees, and marketing. If the event is later canceled, postponed, materially altered, or revealed as fraudulent, ticket buyers demand refunds or initiate credit card chargebacks. Because the platform typically acts as the merchant of record or payment facilitator, card networks hold it liable for returning the full ticket value—plus dispute penalties—even though the platform only earned a small percentage fee on the transaction. Attempting to claw back already-disbursed funds from an illiquid or insolvent organizer frequently fails, forcing the platform to cover 100% of the gross ticket volume out of its own balance sheet. During widespread disruptions or a single large festival collapse, these unrecoverable liabilities can rapidly wipe out the thin margins earned across thousands of successful events and trigger punitive card-network chargeback thresholds.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Paying merchants before the event shifts the fulfillment risk from the merchant to the platform, and the payoff is badly lopsided. The platform usually earns a small fee, often a few percent, but it ends up exposed to the full ticket value until the event actually happens.

When the platform is the merchant of record, the customer's contract and card payment run through it. If a restaurant, venue or organizer cancels, goes bankrupt, or simply doesn't deliver, customers ask for refunds or file chargebacks, and card networks give them months to do it. The platform has to repay them even though it has already passed the money on. Getting it back from a merchant that has spent it or become insolvent is often impossible.

These losses also tend to arrive together. A pandemic, recession or regional disaster can cancel thousands of events at once, which turns small individual exposures into a liquidity crisis. COVID-19 showed this in 2020, when Eventbrite and others faced huge refund liabilities on advance payouts they had already made. The long gap between sale and service makes it worse, because liabilities build up quietly before any failure becomes visible.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Paying merchants before an event takes place exposes hospitality ticketing platforms to severe deferred-delivery risk because customers pay weeks or months before the service is actually rendered. If an organizer cancels the event, fails to deliver the promised experience, commits fraud, or becomes insolvent before the event date, attendees will demand refunds or file "services not rendered" chargebacks through their card issuers. Because the platform has already disbursed the ticket proceeds, it may be unable to claw back those funds from a cash-strapped or vanished merchant. Under card network rules and payment processing agreements, the ticketing platform—especially when acting as the merchant of record or payment facilitator—remains financially liable for covering those refunds and chargeback fees out of its own capital. This creates an asymmetric risk profile: the platform earns only a small percentage commission on each ticket, yet assumes 100% of the gross ticket value as downside liability, meaning a single cancelled festival or bankrupt venue can wipe out months of profit or threaten the platform's solvency.

points.why: The response explains that early payout can leave the platform covering refunds and chargeback fees when it cannot recover the proceeds from a defaulting merchant.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Paying merchants before an event turns ticket proceeds into an unsecured advance. If the event is canceled or the merchant fails to deliver, customers may be owed refunds or file chargebacks after the platform has already released the money. If the merchant has spent the funds, gone insolvent, or disappeared, the platform may have to cover those claims itself.

The downside is disproportionate to the platform’s earnings. It may keep only a small fee per ticket but face claims for the full ticket price across an entire event, all at once. Holding proceeds until the event takes place keeps funds available if customers need to be refunded.
